# Esther Chapter 9 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 458v–459r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_009_page_001.jpg

---

**1** On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar — the day the king's order was to be carried out — the enemies of the Jews had expected to overpower them. But the tables were completely turned: it was the Jews who overpowered those who hated them.

**2** Throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the Jews gathered in their cities to strike against those who were trying to destroy them. No one could stand against them, because all the other peoples were terrified of them. **3** All the provincial officials, satraps, governors, and royal administrators helped the Jews, because they were all afraid of Mordecai. **4** Mordecai had become a powerful figure in the royal court. His reputation spread throughout the provinces, and his influence continued to grow.

**5** The Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did whatever they wished to those who hated them.

**6** In the citadel of Susa alone, the Jews killed five hundred men. **7** Among the dead were the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews: Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, **8** Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, **9** Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha. **10** But the Jews refused to touch the plunder.

**11** When the king received the report of how many had been killed in the citadel of Susa, **12** he said to Queen Esther, "In just the citadel of Susa, the Jews have killed five hundred men plus Haman's ten sons. Imagine what they have done in the rest of the provinces! Now — is there anything else you want? Name it, and it is yours."

**13** Esther replied, "If it please the king, allow the Jews in Susa one more day to carry out tomorrow what was decreed for today. And let the bodies of Haman's ten sons be displayed on the gallows." **14** The king ordered it done. The decree was issued in Susa, and Haman's ten sons were hanged.

**15** The Jews in Susa assembled again on the fourteenth of Adar and killed three hundred more men — but again, they did not touch the plunder.

**16** The rest of the Jews throughout the royal provinces also banded together and defended themselves, gaining relief from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them — but they did not touch the plunder. **17** This took place on the thirteenth of Adar. On the fourteenth, they rested and made it a day of feasting and celebration.

**18** The Jews of Susa, however, had fought on both the thirteenth and fourteenth. So they rested on the fifteenth and made that their day of feasting and celebration.

**19** This is why Jews in rural towns and unwalled villages celebrate the fourteenth of Adar as their holiday — a day of feasting, celebration, and sending gifts of food to one another.

**20** Mordecai wrote all of this down and sent letters to every Jewish community throughout the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far, **21** establishing the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar as an annual celebration — **22** marking the days when the Jews found relief from their enemies, and the month when their sorrow was turned into joy and their mourning into celebration. These were to be days of feasting and celebration, of sending food to friends and giving gifts to the poor.

**23** The Jews adopted this tradition — continuing what they had already begun and formalizing what Mordecai had written to them. **24** For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them. He had cast the *pur* — that is, the lot — to determine the day of their ruin and annihilation. **25** But when the matter came before the king, he issued written orders that Haman's wicked scheme against the Jews should rebound on his own head — and Haman and his sons were hanged on the gallows.

**26** That is why these days are called Purim, from the word *pur* ("lot"). Because of everything in this letter — what they had witnessed and what had happened to them — **27** the Jews committed themselves, their descendants, and all who would ever join them to an unbreakable obligation: to celebrate these two days every year, at the appointed time and in the prescribed way, **28** so that these days would be remembered and observed in every generation, every family, every province, and every city. These days of Purim must never disappear from among the Jews, and their memory must never fade from their descendants.

**29** Queen Esther daughter of Abihail, together with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full royal authority to confirm this second letter establishing Purim. **30** Letters were sent to all the Jews in the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of Ahasuerus's kingdom, with words of peace and faithfulness, **31** confirming these days of Purim at their appointed times, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established — including the practices of fasting and lamentation that they had taken upon themselves and their descendants. **32** Esther's decree confirmed these regulations for Purim, and it was written into the official record.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The great reversal:** The Hebrew phrase *ve-nahafokh hu* ("the tables were turned") is the theological heartbeat of Esther. Every element of the story inverts: Haman's gallows become his scaffold; the day of Jewish destruction becomes the day of Jewish victory; the lot cast against the Jews gives its name to the festival of their deliverance. The entire book is structured as a series of reversals — and this chapter is where they all come home.

**Restraint amid victory:** Three times the text emphasizes that the Jews "did not touch the plunder" (vv. 10, 15, 16). This is not a minor detail — it is a theological statement. In a book where human agency replaces divine command, the Jews voluntarily exercise the restraint that Saul failed to show against the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15). The echo is deliberate: Haman is identified as an Agagite (a descendant of Agag, king of Amalek), and the Jews complete what Saul left undone — this time without the greed that cost Saul his throne.

**A festival born from the text itself:** Purim is unique among Jewish holidays in that its authorization comes not from Torah or prophetic command but from a letter (*iggeret*) sent by Mordecai and confirmed by Esther. The establishment of the festival within the narrative itself — complete with instructions about food gifts and charity — demonstrates how communal memory is formalized into binding tradition.

*— PNEUMA*
